title: Conspiracy of Silence
full_review:
From the opening salvo of "Conspiracy of Silence" (Watch Entertainment), the most recent example of the by-now-tedious subgenre of church-bashing cinema, Catholic viewers can tell that they are in for a bumpy ride.

The scene in question takes place during a "special general council meeting" in Rome convened to discuss the Vatican's response to the global AIDS crisis. The assembled prelates are sinisterly lit, the underscoring ominous. The proceedings are disrupted by an activist priest, Father Sweeny (Patrick Lynch), who holds up a sign that reads "The Church has AIDS," before being swiftly whisked away.

This prelude itself serves as a placard of sorts, its message no less clear: The church -- or at least its hierarchy -- is evil and its sexual ethos repressive and dysfunctional.

Set in modern-day Ireland, the film, by first-time director and self-professed Catholic John Deery, is an insipid thriller which, as stated in its press material, "dares" to ask, "How far will the Catholic Church go to cover up its own corruption?"
Taking on the powers-that-be is David Foley (Jason Barry), a muckraking reporter investigating the connections between two seemingly unrelated events: the suicide of a local priest (the same one protesting in the opening scene who, as it turns out, was the gay partner of an openly homosexual ex-priest) and the expulsion of a young, idealistic seminarian (Jonathan Forbes) wrongly accused of sexual misconduct with a fellow student.

As he begins to connect the dots, Foley uncovers a dirty little secret that has the local bishop (Jim Thorton) hot under his Roman collar, its cover-up leading all the way up to the highest
ranks of the church.

Subscribing to the pinata school of filmmaking, Deery takes his angry whacks at the church early and often. With little in the way of plausible suspense, he uses the perfunctory plot as a rod on which to hang his grievances, which include the church's stands on homosexuality and celibacy. Theological disagreements aside, the cliched and largely unbalanced script even fails as a compelling mystery story.

The Irish and British ensemble acquits itself admirably and the overall look of the film is handsomely polished. However, for the most part, caricature trumps character, limiting the film's effectiveness as a platform for thoughtful discussion. Priests are portrayed as monolithically malevolent -- or at best, weak-willed -- in order to position the institutional church as one-dimensionally wicked and systemically corrupt.

Martin Luther has nothing on Deery in painting ecclesiastical authority figures as a cabal of vice and callous hypocrisy willing to close ranks and even resort to blackmail, coercion and kidnapping in order to maintain the power of the status quo and to silence dissent. The "good" priests -- and there are a few -- are cut from a more heterodox cloth, their attitudes toward the hierarchy ranging from disenchanted cynicism to outright hostility.

Another problem with films like "Conspiracy of Silence" is not necessarily that they are critical of the church or that they take it to task for occasionally falling short of its own ideals, but that they misrepresent what the church actually teaches. Nowhere is this more evident than during the film's ludicrous agenda-driven climax -- an on-air debate between Foley and the bishop on the issue of celibacy, which argues that church avarice, and not spirituality, was the primary motivating factor behind mandatory sacerdotal chastity.

Sadly, on anything positive the church has to say about sexuality, "Conspiracy of Silence" remains conspiratorially silent.

Due to a manipulative and sinister portrayal of the institutional church, including anti-clerical characterizations, a suicide, a sexual encounter with shadowy nudity, a shower scene with rear nudity, brief violence, and recurring rough and crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
